passage: "Listen to that," said Nani, laughing. "Wasim thumps his bowl, and now Arnab thumps his." "Watch, he waits for Wasim first," said Mummy, setting down the dal. The two boys grinned at each other. Wasim clapped. Arnab clapped a moment later, not knowing why. "Now Wasim shakes his head at the beans." "And Arnab shakes his head too, with a full mouth!" The baby in Nani's lap only chewed a rusk and watched.

qa.q: What did Arnab do after Wasim thumped his bowl?
qa.a: Arnab thumped his own bowl, and later clapped after Wasim clapped.

qa.q: What does Arnab's waiting for Wasim before each action suggest about why Arnab does it?
qa.a: It suggests Arnab is simply copying the boy beside him, with no idea of rules or approval; doing what Wasim does feels natural to a toddler.

qa.q: How could a caregiver make use of this copying in a gentle way?
qa.a: A caregiver could show a calm action, such as patting the table softly or eating a bean, and let the toddlers copy that, since imitation is how they learn.

qa.q: How might the baby in Nani's lap be experiencing the banging and clapping?
qa.a: The baby chews a rusk and watches, so the noise is something to look at rather than something to join yet.

grounding: A toddler imitates the child beside them, banging and clapping only because the other did, with no notion of rules.

passage: Toddler room note, Tuesday. At snack Lakshmi pushed her banana slices away and screwed up her face. Trisha, who had eaten banana happily all week, looked across, pushed her own plate away and made the same face. Then Imran did it too. Only Deepa kept eating, without looking up. None of them seemed to be objecting to the fruit itself. I put the banana back without comment and will offer it again tomorrow. — Anita, toddler room carer

qa.q: Who kept eating banana while the others pushed their plates away?
qa.a: Deepa kept eating, without looking up.

qa.q: Why did Trisha push away banana after eating it happily all week?
qa.a: Trisha seems to have copied Lakshmi's face and gesture rather than disliking the banana, since nothing else about the fruit had changed.

qa.q: What did Anita choose to do about the refused banana, and why is that a sensible choice?
qa.a: Anita put the banana back without comment and planned to offer it again tomorrow, which avoids making the refusal a battle for children who are only imitating.

qa.q: What might snack time be like for Deepa, who kept eating while three others refused?
qa.a: Deepa may be the child least affected by the others; eating without looking up suggests Deepa is absorbed in the food rather than in what the group does.

grounding: Toddlers refuse a food because the child beside them does, showing pure imitation with no idea of approval.

passage: Monday. Devika refused the green bottle at water time. "Kiran and Mihir and Tara have blue ones," she said, clutching her blue lid. Tara shrugged and went on drinking. Thursday. The four of them played shop. Devika said the rule was that everyone must be the shopkeeper, and Mihir agreed at once; Kiran frowned but said nothing. Next Tuesday. The teacher gave out red and yellow ribbons for the dance. Devika looked at Kiran's, took the same colour, and danced the same step a beat behind him, smiling only when he smiled back.

qa.q: Why did Devika clutch the blue lid on Monday?
qa.a: Devika clutched the blue lid because Kiran, Mihir and Tara have blue ones.

qa.q: What might Devika feel when her ribbon matches Kiran's and Kiran smiles back?
qa.a: Devika seems to feel safe and included; smiling only when Kiran smiles suggests sameness reassures Devika.

qa.q: What small step could the teacher take to help Devika feel safe while trying something different?
qa.a: The teacher could let Devika keep one thing the same as the group and try one small difference beside another child, so being different is not lonely.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel about Devika's shop rule that everyone must be the shopkeeper?
qa.a: Kiran frowns but says nothing, which suggests Kiran is unhappy with the rule but would rather keep the game going than argue.

grounding: A child wants the same bottle, game rule and dance step as the group because sameness feels safe, shown across three days.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library with ten minutes left before the buses. The teacher showed a new step: two claps and a jump. Kunal did it at once, then Ravi and Sana. Yogesh stood still, watching their feet. "Everybody is doing the same one," he whispered, and copied them, one beat late. Only Hema kept her old arm wave. Yogesh glanced at her, edged closer to Kunal, and did not look at Hema again until the bell rang.

qa.q: Why was the sports-day dance practised in the tiny library?
qa.a: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh copy the new step one beat late?
qa.a: Yogesh saw everybody doing the same step and whispered that they were all doing the same one, so copying felt safer than standing out; the feeling is a wish to belong.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Yogesh that keeps both belonging and difference possible?
qa.a: The teacher could say that a group can share one dance and still let a person add a small touch, so being different is not the same as being left out.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hema to keep her arm wave while the others do the new step?
qa.a: Hema may feel a little alone yet sure of her own step; Hema keeps going even when Yogesh glances over and edges away.

grounding: A child insists on the same dance step as the group, and time pressure in a cramped room makes sameness feel safer than difference.

passage: Monday. Jasleen hummed the theme of her favourite dragon-baker cartoon at lunch. Yash grinned. "That is for babies!" Three boys laughed; Meera looked at her tiffin and said nothing. Wednesday. Yash asked who still watched it. "Not me," said Jasleen. "I stopped ages ago." The laughing moved on to someone else, and her shoulders dropped. Saturday. At home she watched the new episode with the volume low, one ear on the door. The dragon burned the bread again. She smiled, then felt a small pinch, as if she had left something outside in the rain.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say when Yash asked who still watched the cartoon?
qa.a: Jasleen said "Not me" and claimed she had stopped ages ago.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Jasleen have on Wednesday and on Saturday?
qa.a: Relief when the laughing moves on, and a small pinch of having betrayed something she loves, like leaving a favourite thing out in the rain.

qa.q: What choice could help Jasleen enjoy the cartoon without being mocked?
qa.a: Jasleen could quietly tell Meera, who said nothing, that it is still a favourite; one person who knows makes the taste feel less like a secret.

qa.q: How might Meera feel as the boys laugh at Jasleen?
qa.a: Meera may feel uneasy; looking at her tiffin and saying nothing suggests she does not want to join in but also does not want to be the next target.

grounding: A child stops admitting a liked cartoon after others mock it, feeling relief at not standing out and a small betrayal of self.

passage: Sit, beta, and let your Nani tell you something silly. I was ten, and in those days everyone called me Vinita. I loved humming an old radio song about a boatman. Then our class laughed at it. Jahnavi, the loudest girl, called it a grandmother's song, and the others giggled while one boy stared at his desk. After that I told everyone I liked the new film songs. I felt light, as if I had put down a heavy bag. But every evening I hummed the boatman song into my pillow. Years later Jahnavi told me she had known every word of it too.

qa.q: Which song did Vinita hum before the class laughed?
qa.a: Vinita hummed an old radio song about a boatman.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say she liked the new film songs instead?
qa.a: Vinita wanted the laughing to stop; the relief was like putting down a heavy bag, though Vinita went on humming the boatman song into the pillow, so a small loss stayed behind.

qa.q: What small step could have let Vinita keep the song without being mocked?
qa.a: Vinita could have hummed it near one kind listener, or said calmly that it was a favourite whatever the others thought.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when calling the song a grandmother's song while knowing every word of it?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably felt the same pull to fit in, hiding a real liking behind a joke, which shows other children may be hiding private tastes too.

grounding: A child hides a liked song once others mock it, feeling relief at not standing out and a private sense of betraying oneself.

subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]
passage: "What is eight times seven?" asked Ms Iyer. "Fifty-four!" called half the class. "Fifty-four," said Keerthana, firmly. Uma's pencil hovered over the number she had written. "Uma?" "Um... fifty-four?" "Are you sure?" Ms Iyer's eyebrows lifted. Uma stared at her notebook. "Fifty-six is what I wrote," Uma mumbled, "but everyone said..." Rohan, at the back, had said nothing at all. "Thank you for telling us, Uma. Class, let us count in eights together." Keerthana's ears went red.

qa.q: What number had Uma written in her notebook?
qa.a: Uma had written fifty-six.

qa.q: What was Uma thinking when saying fifty-four aloud?
qa.a: Uma doubted the written answer because most of the class said something else; agreeing felt easier than being the lone voice, even though Uma privately had fifty-six.

qa.q: What could Uma try next time when the class says something different from an answer Uma is sure about?
qa.a: Uma could say "I got fifty-six, can we check?" or show the working, so the answer is tested rather than dropped.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Ms Iyer suggests counting in eights?
qa.a: Keerthana may feel embarrassed; going red suggests she was sure and has now been shown wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: A child who knew the right answer changes it when most of the class says otherwise, because self-doubt feels easier than being the lone voice.

subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]
passage: My name is Sharmila and this is about the day I changed a right answer. Sir asked, "Is a bat a bird or a mammal?" I knew it was a mammal because we had read about it. But Urmila said bird, and then most hands went up for bird. I lifted my hand for bird too. My tummy felt heavy. Only Kabir kept his hand still and said nothing. Later Sir told us it was a mammal and I wanted to hide under the desk. Urmila laughed at herself, but I did not laugh. I had known, and I let the others decide.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask about the bat?
qa.a: Sir asked whether a bat is a bird or a mammal.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila raise a hand for bird?
qa.a: Because most of the class chose bird, Sharmila trusted the crowd over private knowledge; the heavy tummy shows an uneasy, doubting feeling.

qa.q: What might Sharmila try at the moment the hands go up?
qa.a: Sharmila could keep the hand down or say "I read that it is a mammal", giving the class a second answer to think about.

qa.q: What might Kabir have been feeling by keeping a hand still and saying nothing?
qa.a: Kabir may have been unsure, or sure and afraid of speaking up; not joining the bird hands suggests unwillingness to follow the crowd without knowing.

grounding: A child who knew the right answer changes it after others answer, feeling heavy afterwards for letting the group decide.

passage: Rosa's coat was an old one, with the sleeves rolled twice. At the school gate in Hamburg, Oskar tugged a sleeve and laughed, "Did you get that from a museum?" Three boys giggled. Two girls looked away. Rosa pulled her hands inside the sleeves and said nothing, her ears burning. At recess she took the coat off and stood in the cold in her thin jumper, and Oskar blinked, as if this was not what he had wanted. Only Lena, near the fence, held out a scarf, and Rosa took it without a word.

qa.q: How were the sleeves of Rosa's coat arranged?
qa.a: The sleeves of Rosa's coat were rolled twice.

qa.q: What might Rosa feel when standing in the cold without the coat?
qa.a: Rosa feels ashamed and quietly resentful; taking the coat off shows a wish to make the difference vanish, even at the cost of warmth.

qa.q: What could a bystander or adult do when someone is laughed at for old clothes?
qa.a: A bystander or adult could stay beside the person, give a kind gesture as Lena did, or speak up calmly to say the joke is not funny.

qa.q: How might Lena see Rosa in that moment?
qa.a: Lena seems to have seen someone cold and hurt rather than someone funny, and chose one small kind act by offering the scarf.

grounding: A child in an old coat is laughed at, shrinks, and takes the coat off to hide the difference until one kind gesture arrives.

passage: In the school canteen Tarun opened his dented steel tiffin. Brown bread, with jam his mother had made. "Is that from a science lab?" said Lokesh, and Piyush snorted. Zoya kept eating, eyes down. Tarun closed the lid halfway. "It is nice," he said, too quietly. The duty teacher was scolding juniors at the far table. Tarun ate three bites in the shadow of the lid, then dropped the rest in the dustbin, and told himself he did not care about their faces. He walked out before the bell, and nobody noticed.

qa.q: What did Tarun's tiffin contain?
qa.a: Tarun's tiffin had brown bread with jam his mother had made.

qa.q: What does Tarun's dropping the bread in the dustbin suggest about how Tarun feels?
qa.a: Tarun feels embarrassed and a bit resentful; throwing the food away and telling himself he does not care hides how much the laughing stung.

qa.q: What could Tarun try before the next lunch break?
qa.a: Tarun could sit with someone kind, or tell the duty teacher what happened; one ally makes being different easier.

qa.q: What might Zoya be feeling while eating with eyes down?
qa.a: Zoya may feel uncomfortable and unwilling to join the laughing, but also afraid of becoming the next target.

grounding: A child with a homemade tiffin is laughed at and quietly copies the group by hiding the food, learning that difference has a price.

passage: Friday, 11:40 pm. Said "bro, that is lit" four times today and nobody blinked, so I guess I sound right now. Suraj's group, six of us, sat on the low wall outside school. Suraj dared us to bunk the last period and ride to the flyover. Everyone said yes in a row, Ankit, then Dev, then me. Only Tanvi said "I have a Maths test" and they laughed, and Tanvi went in. I wanted to say I did not want to, but my mouth said "let's go". We went. I laughed the whole way but my stomach was tight. Everyone knows my new slang. Does anyone know me? — Yash

qa.q: Who dared the group to bunk the last period?
qa.a: Suraj dared them to bunk the last period and ride to the flyover.

qa.q: Why did Yash's mouth say "let's go" when Yash wanted to say no?
qa.a: Yash wanted to belong to Suraj's group; the tight stomach shows the doubt stayed private behind the laughing.

qa.q: What choice at the wall might have kept Yash in the group without going along?
qa.a: Yash could have said "not the bunking, but I am in for the flyover another day", or walked in with Tanvi; a light no with one ally is easier to keep.

qa.q: What might Tanvi have felt when saying "I have a Maths test" and walking in while the others laughed?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt awkward at being laughed at but steady enough to accept it, giving a calm reason without blaming anyone.

grounding: A teenager takes up the group's slang and goes along with a risky dare to belong, while feeling private doubt and unknown.

passage: My name is Farida, and I remember the exact tone of Rafiq's voice at the gate. "Everyone is skipping the last two periods. You coming or what?" Five of them stood in a half-circle, Rafiq in the middle, the rest nodding. Nasreen looked at her shoes. Nobody said what would happen if I refused, but Rafiq added, "We'll just tell you about it after." That was the threat. My chest tightened as if I would lose the whole group, not just an afternoon. I said, "Not today, I have to submit my file." It was true, and a little less than the whole truth. They left. I sat in class with my heart thudding, and an hour later Nasreen sent one 👍.

qa.q: What did Rafiq add after asking whether Farida was coming?
qa.a: Rafiq added, "We'll just tell you about it after."

qa.q: Why did the sentence "We'll just tell you about it after" feel like a threat to Farida?
qa.a: It hinted at being left out, so Farida feared losing the whole group; the social cost felt bigger than the skipped classes and brought a tight, anxious feeling.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped, and what could Farida add next time?
qa.a: Farida gave a plain reason and stayed in class; next time Farida could also tell a trusted adult or Nasreen how pressured it felt.

qa.q: What might Nasreen have been feeling when looking at her shoes and later sending a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Nasreen may have shared the doubts but not dared to say no in front of the group; the thumbs-up later suggests quiet support for Farida.

grounding: A teenager is told that skipping class is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion, and the social threat feels bigger than the act.

passage: Coach's note, Tuesday practice. I noticed Karthik hanging back at the nets while Lokesh and three others whispered near the pavilion. Later Karthik told me Lokesh had said, "Everyone vapes, don't be the odd one out, or the trip group won't include you." Karthik was not sure what to do and was ashamed of seeming scared. I told him it was fair to say no and that telling me was not wrong. That evening I called his parents and the school counsellor, who will speak with the group about vaping this week. Karthik looked lighter when he left the ground. — Coach Malik

qa.q: What did Lokesh say would happen if Karthik did not join?
qa.a: Lokesh said the trip group would not include Karthik.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when telling the coach?
qa.a: Karthik felt unsure and ashamed of seeming scared; looking lighter afterwards shows relief at having told an adult.

qa.q: What turning point helped Karthik, and what was the sensible follow-up?
qa.a: Karthik telling Coach Malik was the turning point, and the coach responded the same evening by calling the parents and the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see the moment when Karthik hangs back from the group?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel the group needs everyone to join to feel united, so a refusal could feel like a threat to belonging rather than a judgement of the group.

grounding: A teenager is told that vaping is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion, and a coach helps by responding the same day.

subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]
passage: Note for Thursday's meeting with the school counsellor, from Pallavi. My son Kunal has started saying "cringe" and "no cap" at dinner, pushes his hair over his eyes, and plays a band I do not know. Three new friends, Arjun, Dev and Sameer, come by after school. On Monday I said, "What is this noise?" and Kunal went silent and shut his door. On Tuesday I asked him to play me his favourite song in the car and tell me what he likes in it. He explained for ten minutes, and even sang a line. I will keep asking about the friends, and not laugh at the words.

qa.a: Pallavi asked Kunal to play his favourite song and tell what he likes in it.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Pallavi said "What is this noise?" on Monday?
qa.a: Kunal likely felt mocked and pulled away, which is why the door closed; ridicule pushes a teen closer to the group that accepts the new taste.

qa.q: What choice did Pallavi make on Tuesday that worked better than ridicule?
qa.a: Pallavi asked with curiosity and listened, which let Kunal explain for ten minutes and sing a line.

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling when explaining the band to Pallavi and singing a line?
qa.a: Kunal probably feels relieved and proud at being taken seriously, and closer to Pallavi than after the Monday remark.

grounding: A parent notices new slang, music and friends, and finds that steady curiosity works better than ridicule.

subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]
passage: Sunday night. My daughter Irawati came home with a new phrase, "that's so mid", and a new circle from art class, Meher and Ishaan and a girl everyone calls Sunny. They hummed a song I have never heard. At lunch I laughed and said, "Mid? Like middle?" Her fork stopped. She took her plate to her room. I felt stupid. Tonight I knocked and asked her to teach me three of the new words. She rolled her eyes, but she taught me, and then told me Meher does funny voices and Ishaan draws maps of imaginary towns. Note to self: ask, do not mock. She is still the same girl. — Sangeeta

qa.q: Which phrase did Irawati bring home?
qa.a: Irawati brought home the phrase "that's so mid".

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling after Irawati took her plate to her room?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt stupid and regretful about having laughed; the knock on the door that night shows a wish to repair it.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do that opened the conversation, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sangeeta knocked and asked Irawati to teach three new words, which shows interest instead of ridicule and lets Irawati be the expert.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Irawati when Sangeeta laughed at "mid" in front of everyone at lunch?
qa.a: Irawati probably felt embarrassed and dismissed, which fits stopping the fork and leaving the table; a new identity is easily hurt by mockery.

grounding: A parent notices new slang and a new social circle, and curiosity works better than ridicule, which pushes the teen away.

passage: So Reena, you know how it went behind the canteen? Six of us, and Tamanna announces we should skip science and watch the match at the tea stall. Everyone was hyped. I just said, "Nah, not for me, have fun though," in a light way, no speech. Two people rolled their eyes, and Tamanna said, "Your loss." My face went hot. Then you said, "Actually, I'm heading to class too," and we walked off together. I have never been so grateful for one person. We sat in the back row and laughed at how nervous we both were. On Monday the group was fine with me, mostly. Not bad for Seema, right?

qa.q: What did Tamanna suggest the group do?
qa.a: Tamanna suggested they skip science and watch the match at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling after Reena said "Actually, I'm heading to class too"?
qa.a: Seema felt grateful and relieved; having one person who agreed made the refusal far easier to keep than saying no alone.

qa.q: What made Seema's refusal work without a fight?
qa.a: Seema kept it light and short, "Nah, not for me, have fun though", with no lecture, and accepted one ally instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt before speaking up after Seema's refusal?
qa.a: Reena may have felt just as nervous as Seema and been waiting for someone else to say no first; the shared laughing later suggests the nervousness was mutual.

grounding: A teenager says a relaxed no without a lecture, and one ally who feels the same makes dissent easy to sustain.

passage: I was in the bunk above Leela's on the school trip, so I saw the whole thing. Around ten, four boys from the next room knocked and said they were sneaking out to wander the town. Wasim was on the floor with a book. He said, "Not for me, thanks, I'm going to sleep," smiling, like he was declining an extra biscuit. Someone said "boring". Wasim just shrugged. Then Leela said from her bunk, "Same, honestly," and Wasim looked up and grinned. The boys left. I said nothing, but I lay there thinking Wasim seemed calm, and a lot less lonely once Leela spoke.

qa.q: Where were the four boys planning to go?
qa.a: The four boys were sneaking out to wander the town.

qa.q: What does Wasim's smile while declining suggest about how Wasim feels?
qa.a: The smile and shrug suggest Wasim feels calm and comfortable refusing, and the grin at Leela's "Same, honestly" shows relief and gratitude at having an ally.

qa.q: How could the person on the top bunk support Wasim and Leela next time?
qa.a: The narrator could speak up too, saying "same" out loud, since each extra voice makes dissent easier and less lonely.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt when saying "Same, honestly" from the bunk?
qa.a: Leela may have wanted to back Wasim and to avoid being seen as boring, and speaking from the bunk suggests a small, easy way to join without any drama.

grounding: A teenager gives a relaxed no thanks, not for me, and a second person's agreement makes dissent easier, told through an observer.

passage: By the third week in the girls' hostel, Disha no longer said she liked sleeping at eleven. At one in the morning the common room was full of instant noodles and a debate about whether the warden was a tyrant. Nirmala was the loudest, and everyone agreed. Disha yawned into her sleeve, said "True, true," and stayed until three. In the mirror next morning, someone she barely knew looked back, with the hostel's opinions and her own dark circles.

qa.a: The girls were debating whether the warden was a tyrant.

qa.q: What small choice could Disha make the next night to keep both belonging and her own view?
qa.a: Disha could go to bed at her usual time like Kavya and Sonal did, and say one honest, mild sentence about the water shortage.

grounding: A new college student drifts into hostel habits of late nights and shared opinions, with the peer group becoming a mirror for identity.

passage: Dear Salma, the hostel here is bigger than our whole street. I have started staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor, which I never did at home. Last Saturday some of them slipped out for drinks. I said no the first time, but now I say "maybe next week" because saying no again feels like a wall. I laugh at jokes about people from our town that I would not have laughed at before. You once told me I always know what I think. Now I check the corridor first. I am not unhappy, just curious who I am becoming. Write soon. — Farida

qa.q: Until what time has Farida been staying up in the corridor?
qa.a: Farida has been staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor.
